From Large Spatiotemporal Data to Urban Insights¶

What We’ll Do Today¶

Across IoT systems, remote sensing, urban platforms, simulation pipelines, and administrative databases, we now have access to huge volumes of spatial and temporal data. Much of it is useful. Some of it is noise. But in either case, the practical challenge is the same:

how do we turn large raw datasets into something usable for analysis, modelling, and digital twins — without wasting computation, memory, and time?

The specific example in this notebook uses climate data, because that is my own area of expertise. But the workflow logic is much broader.

You could swap this dataset for:

  • air quality data
  • mobility traces
  • energy consumption records
  • satellite imagery products
  • sensor networks
  • population or land-use grids

The source changes, the format changes, sometimes even the libraries change — but the core ideas remain the same:

  • inspect data carefully before processing
  • avoid unnecessary work
  • aggregate only what you need
  • choose storage formats that support downstream analysis
  • write code that scales better as data grows

Digital twins depend on data that is not only detailed, but also usable.

In practice, raw data rarely arrives in the form needed for modelling or decision support.
It often needs to be:

  • cleaned
  • subsetted
  • aggregated
  • joined to meaningful spatial units
  • converted into efficient analysis-ready formats

That preparation step is often where most of the real work happens.

If we had unlimited computing resources, one solution would be simple: throw more hardware at the problem.

But most of us do not work with effectively unlimited compute budgets.

So in practice there are two main strategies:

  1. use tools designed for larger-scale computation, such as Dask or PySpark
  2. write more efficient code so we do less unnecessary work in the first place

In this notebook, we focus mainly on the second strategy: efficient data handling and transformation.
If time permits, the second notebook looks at approaches such as vectorisation and Dask.

Today’s Example Workflow¶

To make these ideas concrete, we will work with a real spatiotemporal raster dataset and transform it into a form that is more useful for urban analysis.

Pipeline:

Raw gridded data → inspect structure → spatially aggregate to urban units → store efficiently → explore for analysis

The example here uses gridded climate data for London, which we will aggregate to borough-level units.

The aim is not only to get a final dataset, but to show how to think about:

  • data volume
  • memory use
  • repeated operations
  • file formats
  • spatial aggregation
  • analysis-ready outputs

The Example Data¶

For this workshop, we use a gridded precipitation indicator dataset for London together with London borough boundaries.

The climate dataset is useful here because it has several characteristics that are common in many urban and environmental workflows:

  • it is spatial
  • it is temporal
  • it is stored in a scientific array format
  • it must be transformed before it becomes useful for city-level analysis

So although the example is climate-focused, the same workflow pattern applies far beyond climate.

The main lesson is not “how to work with precipitation data.”
The main lesson is how to work efficiently with large spatiotemporal data.

Context on the Source Data¶

The example dataset comes from the Copernicus Climate Data Store, using a city-scale extreme precipitation product provided as gridded data.

For the workshop, the data has already been prepared and downloaded, so we can focus on processing rather than acquisition.

Each file is a NetCDF (.nc) containing gridded daily values over time.

In a real workflow, acquisition and data organisation are also important parts of the pipeline. Here, we start from the point where raw files are already available locally so we can concentrate on efficient processing and transformation.

Loading & Exploring Gridded Data with xarray¶

What Is xarray?¶

If you work primarily with tabular or vector data, you may not have encountered xarray before. The simplest way to think about it:

xarray is like pandas, but for multi-dimensional data.

A pandas DataFrame is 2D — rows and columns. But gridded climate data is inherently 3D or higher: it has a latitude axis, a longitude axis, and a time axis. Each cell in that 3D cube holds a measurement.

pandas DataFrame:          xarray Dataset:
┌──────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────┐
│  rows × columns  │       │  lat × lon × time       │
│  (2D table)      │       │  (3D+ labelled cube)    │
└──────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────┘

The key advantage: xarray lets you select, slice, and aggregate using dimension names and coordinate labels (e.g., ds.sel(time='2018-07-15')) rather than integer indices. It also integrates with NetCDF, the standard file format for climate and earth science data.

Two core objects:

  • xr.DataArray — a single labelled N-dimensional array (like one variable: e.g., precipitation)
  • xr.Dataset — a collection of DataArrays sharing the same dimensions (like a NetCDF file with multiple variables)

What are we looking at?

  • Dimensions: The axes of our data cube (e.g., time, rlat, rlon — the rotated lat/lon grid)
  • Coordinates: The labels along each dimension (actual lat/lon values, dates)
  • Data variables: The actual measurements (e.g., nrr95p — our extreme precipitation indicator)
  • Attributes: Metadata about the dataset (source, units, description)

Basic xarray Operations¶

xarray lets us select, slice, and aggregate data using dimension names and coordinate labels rather than integer indices. This makes code much more readable and less error-prone.

In [139]:
# Select a single day
one_day = ds['nrr95p'].sel(time='2018-07-15')
print(f"Shape of one day's data: {one_day.shape}")
print(f"Min: {float(one_day.min()):.4f}, Max: {float(one_day.max()):.4f}, Mean: {float(one_day.mean()):.4f}")

Shape of one day's data: (52, 41)
Min: 0.0000, Max: 0.0109, Mean: 0.0004

From xarray to Tabular Data (and When You Should — and Shouldn't)¶

For many downstream tasks (merging with census data, statistical modelling, machine learning), you need tabular data. xarray can convert to pandas DataFrames — but there's an important caveat.

⚠️ Performance Warning: xarray is optimised for operating on large multi-dimensional arrays in its native format. Converting to a pandas DataFrame "melts" the entire grid into rows, which can severely degrade performance and use far more memory. For a file with millions of grid cells × hundreds of time steps, the conversion itself can take a very long time and the resulting DataFrame may not even fit in memory.

Rule of thumb: Do as much work as possible in xarray (selection, aggregation, masking) before converting to pandas. Only convert when you genuinely need tabular operations.

For our dataset this conversion is fine (the files are manageable), but keep this in mind when you scale up to larger grids or longer time series.

In [140]:
# Convert to DataFrame — this "melts" the 3D grid into rows
df_sample = ds.to_dataframe().reset_index()
print(f"Shape: {df_sample.shape}")
print(f"Memory usage: {df_sample.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6:.1f} MB")
df_sample.head()

Notice: The grid data doesn't cover the entire Greater London area — outer boroughs have no data. We need to filter our borough boundaries to only those that actually contain grid points, otherwise we'd have boroughs with no precipitation data in our final dataset.

In [145]:
# Filter to boroughs that actually contain grid points
boroughs_with_data = gpd.sjoin(
    boroughs, grid_gdf, how="inner", predicate="intersects"
).drop_duplicates(subset=[boroughs.geometry.name])

# Keep only the original borough columns (sjoin adds the point columns)
boroughs_with_data = boroughs_with_data[boroughs.columns]

print(f"Boroughs with data coverage: {len(boroughs_with_data)} / {len(boroughs)}")

Memory Management: Why We Explicitly Delete Large Objects¶

Before moving on, it is worth pausing on memory management, because for large spatiotemporal workflows this is often the difference between a notebook that runs smoothly and one that crashes.

The problem¶

When we work with large datasets, we create many big Python objects along the way:

  • ds, ds_year — xarray datasets loaded from NetCDF
  • ds_clean, ds_year_clean — cleaned / reshaped intermediate datasets
  • agg, agg_year — aggregation results
  • agg_df, agg_year_df — pandas tables for export
  • dfs and df_all — concatenated yearly outputs
  • exploratory objects such as df_sample, grid_gdf, annual_mean, summer_mean

Each of these names points to some object in memory. If we keep references to objects we no longer need, memory usage grows. In a loop over many years, that can eventually lead to slowdowns or even a MemoryError.

How memory management works in CPython¶

In CPython, memory management has two layers:

  1. Reference counting
    Every object keeps track of how many active references point to it.
    When that count drops to zero, the object can usually be reclaimed immediately.

  2. Cyclic garbage collection
    Some objects can reference each other in a cycle, so their reference counts never reach zero even though the program no longer needs them.
    Python’s garbage collector periodically looks for these unreachable cycles and frees them.

So when we write:

del ds_year, ds_year_clean, agg_year, agg_year_df
gc.collect()

we are doing two things:

  • del ... removes the names from the notebook namespace
  • gc.collect() asks Python to immediately run a garbage-collection pass for unreachable cyclic objects

Important idea: del removes the name, not magically the bytes¶

For example, in this notebook:

  • after aggregation, ds_year, ds_year_clean, agg_year, and agg_year_df are no longer needed for the next year
  • after concatenation, dfs is no longer needed once df_all exists
  • after the exploratory section, objects like df_sample, grid_means, grid_gdf, one_day, annual_mean, summer, and summer_mean are just taking up RAM

Deleting those names tells Python: we are done with these objects from our side.

If nothing else still references them, they become reclaimable.

What the garbage collector is doing¶

Conceptually, the garbage collector asks:

“Which objects are still reachable from the live program, and which are no longer reachable?”

Objects still reachable through active variables, containers, or object attributes stay alive.

Objects that are no longer reachable can be collected.

In notebook terms:

  • if df_all points to the final combined table, that object must stay alive
  • if dfs has been deleted and nothing else points to those list elements anymore, those intermediate references can disappear
  • if a chain of objects still references each other internally, but nothing in the notebook can reach them anymore, cyclic GC can reclaim them

Why?¶

The critical section is the yearly loop:

for year in YEARS:
    ...
    ds_year = xr.open_dataset(...)
    ds_year_clean = ...
    agg_year = ...
    agg_year_df = ...
    ...
    del ds_year, ds_year_clean, agg_year, agg_year_df
    gc.collect()

Without the cleanup step, each iteration risks leaving behind large intermediate objects. Even if each year is manageable on its own, 19 years of leftovers are not.

The pattern is:

load -> process -> save -> delete references -> collect

That is one of the simplest and most effective ways to keep RAM usage bounded.

What we can do in Python with gc¶

Python exposes the garbage collector through the built-in gc module.

Useful operations include:

  • gc.collect() Run garbage collection immediately

  • gc.get_count() See the current collection counters

  • gc.get_threshold() See the thresholds that control when automatic GC runs

  • gc.get_stats() Inspect collection statistics

  • gc.set_debug(...) Turn on debugging output for GC activity

  • gc.disable() / gc.enable() Temporarily disable or re-enable automatic cyclic GC

In practice, for data workflows like this notebook, the most useful pattern is usually still:

del large_object_1, large_object_2
gc.collect()

A practical caution¶

Garbage collection helps manage Python objects, but memory behaviour is not always identical to what you see in a system monitor.

Python uses its own memory manager and allocators internally, and a full collection may clear some internal free lists, but freed memory is not guaranteed to appear as an immediate drop in OS-level memory usage.

So the real goal is not “make RAM instantly look empty” — it is:

  • reduce the number of live Python objects
  • avoid carrying unnecessary intermediates
  • keep long loops stable
  • prevent avoidable memory pressure

Aggregation¶

The Problem¶

We need to go from grid cells → borough-level values. But grid cells don't align with borough boundaries — a single 2 km cell can span multiple boroughs. There are several approaches:

Method Description Trade-off
Point-in-polygon Assign each grid centre to the polygon it falls in Simple, but ignores that a 2 km cell covers area across borders
Nearest neighbour Assign polygon the value of the nearest grid point Fast, but same problem — no partial overlap
Area-weighted Weight each grid cell's contribution by how much it overlaps a polygon Accounts for partial overlaps; the standard approach for climate data
Population-weighted Weight by population density within each cell-polygon intersection Better for human impact studies (e.g., "how many people are exposed?")
Economic-weighted Weight by economic activity or asset values Used in damage assessment and insurance applications

No single method is "correct" — the choice should match your research question. For exposure assessment, population-weighted is often preferred. For physical hazard characterisation, area-weighted is standard. For damage estimation, economic-weighted may be more appropriate.

Today we'll use area-weighted aggregation with xagg, which computes fractional overlap weights between grid cells and polygons.

Running xagg on a Single Year¶

Let's first understand the process with one file before we scale up.

In [148]:
# --- Step 1: Prepare the xarray Dataset ---
# xagg needs an xarray Dataset with latitude and longitude as coordinate dimensions

# Load raw data
ds = xr.open_dataset(DATA_DIR / "ldn_tp_2018.nc")

# Clean the grid natively in xarray
ds_clean = (
    ds
    .stack(point=['rlat', 'rlon'])               # 1. Flatten the 2D grid into a 1D list of points
    .dropna(dim='point', subset=['nrr95p'])      # 2. Drop the individual NaN points 
    .set_index(point=['latitude', 'longitude'])  # 3. Swap the index from rlat/rlon to actual lat/lon
    .unstack('point')                            # 4. Reshape back into a spatial grid
)

# Clean up leftover coordinate variables if necessary
if 'rlat' in ds_clean or 'rlon' in ds_clean:
    ds_clean = ds_clean.drop_vars(['rlat', 'rlon'], errors='ignore')
    
ds_clean

# --- Step 2: Compute pixel-polygon overlap weights ---
# This tells xagg what fraction of each grid cell falls in each borough.
# This only needs to be computed ONCE — the grid and boundaries don't change between years.

weightmap = xagg.pixel_overlaps(ds_clean, boroughs_with_data, subset_bbox=True)
print("Weightmap computed — this will be reused for all years.")

# --- Step 3: Aggregate ---
# This applies the weights to compute area-weighted means per borough per day

agg = xagg.aggregate(ds_clean, weightmap)
agg_df = agg.to_dataframe().reset_index()

print(f"Aggregated shape: {agg_df.shape}")

Visualising the Aggregated Result¶

# Compute borough-level annual means for plotting
agg_annual = agg_df.groupby('name')['nrr95p'].mean().reset_index()

# Merge with geometry for mapping
agg_gdf = boroughs_with_data.merge(agg_annual, on='name', how='left')

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 7))

# Left: raw grid points
_grid = ds.to_dataframe().reset_index().dropna().groupby(['latitude','longitude'])['nrr95p'].mean().reset_index()
_grid_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(_grid, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(_grid.longitude, _grid.latitude), crs='EPSG:4326')
boroughs_with_data.plot(ax=axes[0], color='lightgrey', edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.5)
_grid_gdf.plot(ax=axes[0], column='nrr95p', cmap='Reds', markersize=3, legend=True)
axes[0].set_title('Raw Grid Points (2 km)')

# Right: aggregated to boroughs
agg_gdf.plot(ax=axes[1], column='nrr95p', cmap='Reds', edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.5, legend=True)
axes[1].set_title('Area-Weighted Aggregation to Boroughs')

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel('Longitude')
    ax.set_ylabel('Latitude')

plt.suptitle('Grid → Borough: nrr95p Mean, London 2018', fontsize=14)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Aggregation Pitfalls¶

Spatial aggregation is not neutral — results depend on the units and resolution used.

  • MAUP: changing boundary size or shape can change the pattern
  • Resolution mismatch: small boroughs may only overlap a few grid cells
  • Edge effects: partial overlaps can affect boundary areas

Takeaway: aggregation is a modelling choice, so be explicit about boundaries, support, and limitations.

In [151]:
# Check: how many grid cells contribute to each borough?
# This helps assess reliability of the aggregation

_grid_check = ds.to_dataframe().reset_index().dropna().groupby(['latitude','longitude']).first().reset_index()
_grid_check_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    _grid_check, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(_grid_check.longitude, _grid_check.latitude), crs='EPSG:4326'
)

cells_per_borough = (
    gpd.sjoin(boroughs_with_data[['name','geometry']], _grid_check_gdf, how='left', predicate='intersects')
    .groupby('name')
    .size()
    .reset_index(name='n_grid_cells')
    .sort_values('n_grid_cells')
)

print("Grid cells per borough (fewest first):")
print(cells_per_borough.to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nBoroughs with ≤ 3 grid cells: {(cells_per_borough['n_grid_cells'] <= 3).sum()}")
print("(Results for these boroughs should be interpreted with caution.)")

del _grid_check, _grid_check_gdf
gc.collect()

A Design Principle: Separate Geometry from Data¶

When working with large spatiotemporal datasets, carrying geometry columns everywhere is expensive. A GeoDataFrame with millions of rows and complex polygon geometries uses far more memory than the same data without geometry.

The pattern:

  1. Aggregated data → save as a lightweight table (parquet) with just the borough name, date, and values. No geometry.
  2. Geometry lookup → keep a small, separate GeoDataFrame of borough boundaries that you merge back only when you need to map.

This way, you're never carrying geometry through millions of rows of data processing. You only pay the geometry cost when visualising.

In [152]:
# Prepare the clean output — only name, time, and value columns
output_cols = ['name', 'time', 'nrr95p']
agg_clean = agg_df[output_cols].copy()

print(f"Clean output shape: {agg_clean.shape}")
print(f"Memory: {agg_clean.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6:.2f} MB")
agg_clean.head()

# Save the borough geometry lookup separately — you only need this once
borough_lookup = boroughs_with_data[['name', 'geometry']].copy()
borough_lookup.to_file(GEO_DIR / 'borough_lookup.gpkg', driver='GPKG')

print(f"Borough lookup: {len(borough_lookup)} rows, saved to borough_lookup.gpkg")
print("This small file is all you need to rejoin geometry later.")

# Clean up  objects
del ds, ds_clean, agg, agg_df, agg_annual, agg_gdf, agg_clean
del _grid, _grid_gdf, cells_per_borough
gc.collect()
print("Memory freed.")

Efficient Workflows: Loops, Memory, and Parquet¶

We just processed one year. Now we need to do this for all 19 years (2000–2018).

The Pattern: Process → Save → Free Memory¶

When processing many large files, the key pattern is:

for each file:
    1. Load data
    2. Process (clean, aggregate)
    3. Save result to disk (parquet)
    4. Delete objects from memory (del)
    5. Force garbage collection (gc.collect())

This ensures you never hold more than one year's worth of data in memory at a time. Without steps 4–5, Python may keep old objects in memory, and after processing a few years you could run out of RAM.

Why Parquet?¶

You're probably used to CSV files. Parquet is a columnar storage format that is:

  • Smaller on disk — typically 3–10× smaller than CSV (columnar compression)
  • Faster to read — especially for large datasets and column subsets
  • Type-preserving — dates stay as dates, floats stay as floats (no re-parsing on load)

Let's see the difference. We'll use the raw grid data (before aggregation) to get a meaningful file size comparison:

In [153]:
# CSV vs Parquet comparison — using the raw grid data for a meaningful test
ds_demo = xr.open_dataset(DATA_DIR / "ldn_tp_2018.nc")
df_demo = ds_demo.to_dataframe().reset_index().dropna(subset=['nrr95p'])

print(f"Test dataset: {len(df_demo):,} rows × {len(df_demo.columns)} columns")
print(f"In-memory size: {df_demo.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6:.1f} MB")

# Save as CSV
df_demo.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / 'demo_raw.csv', index=False)

# Save as Parquet
df_demo.to_parquet(OUTPUT_DIR / 'demo_raw.parquet', index=False)

Test dataset: 19,345 rows × 6 columns
In-memory size: 1.1 MB
In [154]:
csv_size = os.path.getsize(OUTPUT_DIR / 'demo_raw.csv') / 1e6
pq_size = os.path.getsize(OUTPUT_DIR / 'demo_raw.parquet') / 1e6

# Time CSV read (average of 3 runs)
csv_times = []
for _ in range(3):
    t0 = time.time()
    _ = pd.read_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / 'demo_raw.csv')
    csv_times.append(time.time() - t0)
csv_time = np.mean(csv_times)

# Time Parquet read (average of 3 runs)
pq_times = []
for _ in range(3):
    t0 = time.time()
    _ = pd.read_parquet(OUTPUT_DIR / 'demo_raw.parquet')
    pq_times.append(time.time() - t0)
pq_time = np.mean(pq_times)

print(f"{'Format':<10} {'Size (MB)':<12} {'Read Time (s)':<15}")
print(f"{'-'*37}")
print(f"{'CSV':<10} {csv_size:<12.2f} {csv_time:<15.4f}")
print(f"{'Parquet':<10} {pq_size:<12.2f} {pq_time:<15.4f}")
print(f"\nParquet is {csv_size/pq_size:.1f}× smaller and {(csv_time* 1000)/(pq_time* 1000):.1f}× faster to read.")

Format     Size (MB)    Read Time (s)  
-------------------------------------
CSV        1.97         0.0078         
Parquet    0.14         0.0014         

Parquet is 14.2× smaller and 5.4× faster to read.

This does not mean Parquet is “worse”. For tiny files, Parquet’s metadata, decoding, and decompression overhead can dominate. Its advantages usually become clearer with larger datasets, repeated analytical reads, preserved data types, and especially when reading only a subset of columns.

In [155]:
import time
import pandas as pd
from statistics import mean

def bench(fn, n=20):
    times = []
    for _ in range(n):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return mean(times)

csv_time = bench(lambda: pd.read_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "demo_raw.csv"))
parquet_time = bench(lambda: pd.read_parquet(OUTPUT_DIR / "demo_raw.parquet"))

print(f"CSV read time: {csv_time:.4f} s")
print(f"Parquet read time: {parquet_time:.4f} s")

CSV read time: 0.0076 s
Parquet read time: 0.0007 s

The Processing Loop¶

Now let's process all years. Notice how we:

  • Use tqdm for a progress bar — essential for long-running loops so you know something is happening
  • Use del + gc.collect() to free memory after each year
  • Reuse the weightmap — the grid-polygon overlaps don't change between years
  • Save only name, time, and nrr95p to parquet — no geometry, no extra coordinates
In [157]:
# NOTE: The weightmap was computed in  and is still in memory.
# If you're restarting from here, you'd need to recompute it first.

for year in tqdm(YEARS, desc="Processing years"):
    file_path = DATA_DIR / f"ldn_tp_{year}.nc"
    ds_year = xr.open_dataset(file_path)
    
    # 2. Clean natively in xarray without converting to pandas
    ds_year_clean = (
        ds_year
        .stack(point=['rlat', 'rlon'])               # Flatten spatial dimensions
        .dropna(dim='point', subset=['nrr95p'])      # Drop NaN grid cells
        .set_index(point=['latitude', 'longitude'])  # Use actual lat/lon
        .unstack('point')                            # Reshape back to grid
    )
    
    # Drop the unused rotated coordinates (replaces .drop(columns=['rlon', 'rlat']))
    ds_year_clean = ds_year_clean.drop_vars(['rlat', 'rlon'], errors='ignore')
    
    # 3. Aggregate using the pre-computed weightmap
    agg_year = xagg.aggregate(ds_year_clean, weightmap)
    agg_year_df = agg_year.to_dataframe().reset_index()[['name', 'time', 'nrr95p']]
    
    # 4. Save to parquet — lightweight, no geometry
    out_path = OUTPUT_DIR / f"ldn_nrr95p_{year}.parquet"
    agg_year_df.to_parquet(out_path, index=False)
    
    # 5. Free memory — critical for long loops!
    del ds_year, ds_year_clean, agg_year, agg_year_df
    gc.collect()

print(f"\nDone! {len(YEARS)} parquet files saved to {OUTPUT_DIR}/")

Understanding the Data: Extreme Events vs Background Noise¶

A key feature of extreme precipitation data: most days are not extreme. The nrr95p variable is 0 on dry days and only exceeds 1.0 when precipitation actually surpasses the 95th percentile threshold. This means averages will be dominated by many near-zero days.

For London (which is famously wet), this means simple averages across boroughs will look very similar. We need to focus on the tail of the distribution — the extreme days — to see meaningful spatial and temporal patterns.

In [162]:
# What fraction of days are "extreme" (nrr95p > 1)?
total_days = len(df)
extreme_days_count = (df['nrr95p'] > 1).sum()
wet_days_count = (df['nrr95p'] > 0).sum()

print(f"Total borough-days: {total_days:,}")
print(f"Days with any precipitation signal (nrr95p > 0): {wet_days_count:,} ({wet_days_count/total_days*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"Extreme days (nrr95p > 1): {extreme_days_count:,} ({extreme_days_count/total_days*100:.1f}%)")

# Count extreme days (nrr95p > 1) per borough per year
threshold = 1.0

extreme_by_year = (
    df[df['nrr95p'] > threshold]
    .groupby(['name', 'year'])
    .size()
    .reset_index(name='extreme_days')
)

# City-wide: average across boroughs per year
city_extreme = extreme_by_year.groupby('year')['extreme_days'].mean()

When Do Extreme Events Happen?¶

In [164]:

Dask: When the Workflow No Longer Fits Comfortably in Memory¶

Why Dask?¶

So far, our London example is small enough that we can load data into memory and process it on a single machine without too much trouble.

But this does not scale very far.

If we increase the scope of the problem, things grow quickly:

  • more cities
  • finer spatial resolution
  • more variables
  • longer time periods

A workflow that is easy at London scale can become tens or hundreds of gigabytes at regional, national, or multi-variable scale. At that point, the usual single-machine pandas approach starts to break down: you run into slowdowns, memory pressure, or outright MemoryErrors.

This is where Dask becomes useful.

Dask is a parallel computing library for Python that helps familiar tools such as pandas, NumPy, and xarray scale beyond a single in-memory workflow. It can run on a laptop using multiple cores, or on larger distributed systems, while keeping a user experience that stays close to the libraries many Python users already know. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

The core idea¶

Instead of loading everything into memory at once, Dask works by splitting a dataset into smaller pieces called chunks. Each chunk is small enough to fit into memory, and Dask processes those chunks piece by piece. Xarray’s Dask integration follows exactly this pattern. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

Dask operations are also usually lazy.

That means when we write an operation, Dask does not immediately execute it. Instead, it builds up a task graph describing the work that needs to be done. The actual computation only happens when we ask for a real result — for example with .compute(), when plotting, or when writing output to disk. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

So the workflow becomes:

pandas / NumPy: load everything -> process everything -> result

Dask: define chunked operations lazily -> build task graph -> compute when needed

For geospatial and climate-style data, this is especially useful because datasets are often:

  • multi-dimensional
  • too large to load all at once
  • naturally separable into chunks across time, space, or variables

So instead of rewriting everything in a completely new framework, we can often keep working with familiar tools:

  • Dask DataFrame for pandas-like tabular workflows
  • Dask Array for NumPy-like array workflows
  • Dask-backed xarray for chunked labelled arrays

This is one of Dask’s biggest strengths: it lets us move from a standard single-machine workflow toward parallel and out-of-core computation without having to completely change how we think about the code. ([docs.dask.org][1])

One important caveat¶

Dask is powerful, but it is not automatically the right answer for every case.

If your data fits comfortably in memory and performance is already fine, then plain pandas / NumPy / xarray may still be the better choice because Dask adds another layer of complexity and overhead. Dask’s own best-practices guide explicitly says this.

In [172]:
import dask.dataframe as dd

Loading Data with Dask¶

Earlier, we loaded each parquet file in a loop, appended to a list, and concatenated? Dask handles this natively.

In [173]:
# Pandas way (from previous approach): load all, concatenate
t0 = time.time()
dfs = [pd.read_parquet(f) for f in sorted(OUTPUT_DIR.glob('ldn_nrr95p_*.parquet'))]
df_pandas = pd.concat(dfs, ignore_index=True)
t_pandas = time.time() - t0
print(f"Pandas: loaded {len(df_pandas):,} rows in {t_pandas:.3f}s")
print(f"Memory: {df_pandas.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6:.1f} MB")

del dfs
gc.collect()

Notice: Dask "loaded" the data almost instantly — but it hasn't read a single byte. It just recorded where the files are and what operations we want. The actual reading happens only when we call .compute().

This is lazy evaluation: build the plan first, execute later.

Working with Dask DataFrames¶

The API is nearly identical to pandas — most operations just work.

In [175]:
# These operations are lazy — no computation yet
ddf['time'] = dd.to_datetime(ddf['time'])
ddf['year'] = ddf['time'].dt.year
ddf['month'] = ddf['time'].dt.month

# This is still lazy
annual_mean = ddf.groupby(['name', 'year'])['nrr95p'].mean()

print("Still lazy — no computation has happened:")
print(type(annual_mean))
annual_mean

Replacing the Loop-Concat Pattern¶

Earlier, we processed each year in a loop:

for year in YEARS:
    ds = xr.open_dataset(f"ldn_tp_{year}.nc")
    # ... process ...
    df.to_parquet(f"ldn_nrr95p_{year}.parquet")
    del ds; gc.collect()

Then loaded them all back:

dfs = [pd.read_parquet(f) for f in parquet_files]
df_all = pd.concat(dfs)

With Dask, the second step becomes trivial — and you can do further analytics without loading everything into memory:

In [177]:
# Dask can compute complex aggregations across all files without loading them all at once
t0 = time.time()

# This reads each partition, computes the aggregation, and combines — all chunked
extreme_summary = (
    ddf[ddf['nrr95p'] > 1]
    .groupby('name')
    .agg({'nrr95p': ['count', 'mean', 'max']})
    .compute()
)

t_agg = time.time() - t0
extreme_summary.columns = ['total_extreme_days', 'mean_intensity', 'max_event']

print(f"Computed in {t_agg:.3f}s")
extreme_summary.sort_values('max_event', ascending=False)

Dask + xarray: Lazy-Loading NetCDF Files¶

Dask also integrates with xarray. Instead of our loop that opens each file one at a time, xarray can open all files at once with lazy loading — it only reads data into memory when you actually compute on it.

In [178]:
# Open all NetCDF files at once with lazy loading via dask
nc_files = sorted(DATA_DIR.glob('ldn_tp_*.nc'))

t0 = time.time()
ds_all = xr.open_mfdataset(
    nc_files,
    combine='by_coords',  # align files along the time dimension
    chunks={'time': 365}  # chunk size — one year per chunk
)
t_open = time.time() - t0

print(f"Opened {len(nc_files)} files in {t_open:.3f}s (lazy — no data loaded yet)")
print(f"Time range: {ds_all.time.values[0]} to {ds_all.time.values[-1]}")
print(f"Total time steps: {len(ds_all.time)}")
ds_all

In [180]:
# Compute the temporal mean across ALL years — lazily
all_years_mean = ds_all['nrr95p'].mean(dim='time')

# Still lazy — let's trigger computation
t0 = time.time()
result_array = all_years_mean.compute()
t_compute = time.time() - t0

print(f"Computed 19-year temporal mean in {t_compute:.3f}s")

# Plot
result_array.plot(figsize=(8, 6), cmap='Reds')
plt.title('Mean 95th Percentile Precipitation — London 2000–2018 (all years via Dask)')
plt.show()

Computed 19-year temporal mean in 0.041s

Compare this to the previous approach: Previously, we had to loop over each file, convert to pandas, aggregate with xagg, save to parquet, and then load them all back. With open_mfdataset + dask, xarray handles the chunking and orchestration for you — and only loads into memory the chunks it needs at any given time.

For operations that stay in the xarray/grid world (temporal means, anomalies, trend computation), this is much cleaner. You'd still need xagg for the spatial aggregation to polygons, but all the pre-aggregation analytics can be done lazily.

When to Use Dask vs Pandas¶

Situation Use
Data fits comfortably in memory pandas — simpler, faster for small data
Data is large but each file fits in memory pandas in a loop (our previous approach pattern) or Dask
Data doesn't fit in memory at all Dask — it handles chunking for you
Complex operations needing full random access pandas — load what you can, sample if needed
Simple aggregations across many files Dask — shines at grouped operations on partitioned data
Grid-level operations on NetCDF archives xarray + Dask via open_mfdataset

Dask has overhead — for small datasets, pandas is faster. Dask's advantage appears when your data is larger than RAM or when you want cleaner code for multi-file processing.

In [181]:
# Direct comparison: same aggregation in pandas vs dask

# Pandas
t0 = time.time()
res_pd = df.groupby('name')['nrr95p'].agg(['mean', 'max']).reset_index()
t_pd = time.time() - t0

# Dask
t0 = time.time()
res_dask = ddf.groupby('name')['nrr95p'].agg(['mean', 'max']).compute().reset_index()
t_dask = time.time() - t0

print(f"Pandas:  {t_pd:.4f}s")
print(f"Dask:    {t_dask:.4f}s")
print(f"\nFor this dataset size, pandas is faster — Dask's advantage is when data doesn't fit in RAM.")

# Verify results are the same
print(f"\nResults match: {np.allclose(res_pd['mean'].values, res_dask['mean'].values, rtol=1e-5)}")

Pandas:  0.0183s
Dask:    0.0532s

For this dataset size, pandas is faster — Dask's advantage is when data doesn't fit in RAM.

Results match: False
  • Dask uses lazy evaluation — it builds a computation graph and only executes when you call .compute()
  • dask.dataframe is nearly a drop-in replacement for pandas, useful when data exceeds RAM
  • xr.open_mfdataset with Dask chunks lets you work with multi-file NetCDF archives without loading everything at once
  • Dask has overhead — for datasets that fit in memory, pandas is usually faster. Use Dask when you need it, not by default.
